newsitem.title: USA: Democrats gain slight edge in state legislatures.
newsitem.headline: Democrats gain slight edge in state legislatures.

text.p: Democrats gained majority control of eight state legislatures in Tuesday's elections, partly offsetting a Republican sweep at the state level two years ago that paralleled Republican victories in Congress.

Democrats apparently will control both legislative chambers in 21 states, while Republicans will dominate in 17 states, according to preliminary results compiled by the National Conference of State Legislatures.
Control of nine legislatures will be split between the parties, with two states still undecided and Nebraska's single legislative chamber nonpartisan.
In Tuesday's voting, Democrats took majority control in eight state legislatures from Republicans, while Republicans captured three chambers formerly dominated by Democrats.

The gains by Democrats indicated only a partial swing in the pendulum from the 1994 election, in which the same Republican tidal wave in the Congress cost Democrats control of 16 legislative chambers.

Despite modest Democratic gains on the state level, voters this year were looking for moderation and a continuation of the status quo, said Richard Ciccarone, a municipal analyst at Van Kampen American Capital in Oakbrook Terrace, Illinois.
"Even though President Clinton wants to lead us over that bridge to the 21st century, voters want the other side of the bridge to look the same," Ciccarone said.
Democrat-controlled state legislatures could provide more support for programmes designed to help schools, as well as soften spreading reforms of welfare programmes, analysts said.

The fact that states will now have a bigger role to play in the funding of social services programmes helped to galvanise groups to pour money into state races, said Rich Jones, director of legislative programmes for National Conference of State Legislatures.
"A lot of that is due to the pivotal policy role state legislatures play," Jones said. "They really are a key battleground for people concerned about policy."
In some states such as Illinois and Michigan where Democrats won control of state houses, candidates for state office "clearly felt (President) Clinton's coattails," Jones said.
But in Florida, a state that gave Clinton a plurality, the state House turned over to the Republicans. In Pennsylvania, another Clinton state, the Republicans expanded their majority.

"The surprising thing was that Clinton's coattails weren't very long in a lot of these states," as voters split their ballots, said John Pelissero, a political science professor at Loyola University Chicago.
According to the conference, Democrats took over the majority in the California, Michigan and Illinois and Nevada state houses, and in the Connecticut, Maine, Tennesee and Vermont state senates.
Republicans gained control of the Florida state house and the Iowa and Washington state senates.

Alan Rosenthal, a political science professor at Rutgers University, said the results pointed to the return of some New England states to the Democratic fold, while the South was firmly divided between the parties.
